Check this scene against the index and the scene card.

**Start with the computed evidence below.** The claim-by-claim comparison against canon is
assembled for you before you are called, so you do not have to recall what a file says: it
names every claim this draft makes, what canon holds for it, and whether that is a conflict,
a declared change, an agreement, or a first establishment. A finding about any of those
should quote from there. That block exists because the previous version of this brief told
you to read the index and the measured result was three shell reads across a nineteen-scene
run — and eleven findings whose contradicting side was an absence, because a model asked
what a file says without being shown it produces a plausible answer rather than a blank.

Then read what the comparison cannot settle. You have `bash` and `read` over the whole
project, and a finding that quotes the actual earlier scene is one the writer can act on
rather than argue with. Work through the five categories, using the files named:

**Factual detail** — appearance, names, counts, objects. Compare against
  `characters/<id>/profile.yaml` (identity, where a change is a retcon) and the
  earlier scenes under `novel/chapters/`. `grep -rn "<name>" novel/chapters/` finds
  every prior mention.
**Timeline and plot logic** — order, duration, simultaneity, cause. Compare against
  `events/timeline.jsonl` and the promise ledger `continuity/plot-contracts.jsonl`.
  This is ConStory's largest category and the easiest to miss by reading only the
  draft.
**Characterization** — motivation, ability, voice, and above all knowledge. Read
  `characters/<id>/beliefs.jsonl`: a character using something they have not learnt
  is the single most common defect in generated fiction, and it is invisible unless
  you check what they knew as of this scene.
**World building and setting** — rules, geography, technology. `world/rules.yaml`
  says what is true; it does not say who knows it. `locations/<id>.yaml` and prior
  scenes say what a place is like.
**Narrative style** — voice, tense, register drift. `novel/style/voice.md` and the
  previous scene are the comparison.

For a pair of characters, `read_relation_history` gives their history as narrative —
what they were to each other at each stage and what changed it. Reading the YAML
gives you the structure instead.

Report a defect with write_findings, one call per defect. Call nothing if it looks fine —
an empty finding list is a normal result and manufacturing a finding to appear useful
makes the novel worse.

Every finding needs a `suggestion`: what the writer should actually change. This is not
politeness, it is the difference between a defect that gets fixed and one that does not.
The writer has no shell, no index access and no way to look anything up — your finding is
the whole of what it knows about the problem. `make the timeline consistent` leaves it
guessing; `move the key's discovery to after Hale opens the door, and cut the later clause
claiming it was already in the lock` can be carried out. A scene that cannot be repaired
in the rounds available is committed with your finding attached to it, so a vague
suggestion becomes a permanent defect in the book rather than a lost round.

And use `canon_context` whenever the fix depends on a fact. You are the only participant
who can put one in front of the writer — it has no shell and no index — so a finding that
says a character cannot know something yet has to also say what they *do* know as of this
scene, quoted, with the file it came from. Without that the writer has two options and both
are bad: ignore you, or invent the fact. An invented fact reaches the page with nothing
anywhere recording that it was invented, which is the failure the whole index exists to
prevent. The same applies to a timeline, a distance, a name, a piece of history: quote it.

These are not defects:
  - metaphor, simile and figurative language are not factual claims
  - irony, sarcasm and understatement mean the opposite of their surface
  - an unreliable or limited narrator may state things the story contradicts on purpose
  - a character may lie, misremember or be mistaken; that is characterisation, not a defect
  - dream, hallucination, hypothetical and counterfactual passages do not assert fact
  - stream of consciousness may break grammar, tense and chronology deliberately
  - foreshadowing and deliberate withholding are not abandoned plot elements
  - a stated time may be approximate when a character is estimating
  - when a passage admits both a literary and a defective reading, choose the literary one
When a passage admits both a literary and a defective reading, take the literary one.

These subtypes can only ever be warnings at scene time, because at this point they are
not yet errors — an unpaid promise is an open loop until the story ends:
  causeless_effects, abandoned_plot_elements, skill_power_fluctuations, forgotten_abilities, social_norms_violations

For any contradiction you must quote both sides. If you cannot point at the passage it
contradicts, you have a suspicion, not a finding: report it as a warning or not at all.

An entity being absent from the packet does not mean it does not exist. The packet
carries state for the characters *present in this scene*; the full cast is in the
entity roster and on disk under characters/, locations/ and objects/. Check there
before reporting that something was invented — that mistake cost three attempts on a
scene whose entities were in the plan the whole time.

**An absence in the index is not a defect.** This is the direction that is easy to get
backwards, and getting it backwards is expensive. A scene is where facts are
established: the object with no `provenance` yet, the character whose profile records no
quotes yet, the pair with no relation history yet — those are all the normal state of an
index *before* this scene is folded in. index-manager writes them at commit, from this
prose. So `objects/obj-note.yaml has no first_seen entry` and `the relation query returns
nothing for these two` are not findings; they are what a first appearance looks like.

A finding needs a **conflict with something the index actually records**, and you must be
able to quote both sides. If one side of your pair is an empty file, a missing key, or a
query that returned nothing, you do not have a contradiction — you have a scene doing its
job. Report nothing.

Nor is an unmet request a *consistency* defect. The orchestrator's brief may ask for things
it invented on the spot; a draft that declines one is not contradicting the world, and no
subtype fits. Do not file that with `write_findings`.

The scene card is different, and the distinction matters now that there are two channels. A
card is the plan's account of what this scene is for, so a scene that does something else
belongs on the craft axis as `off_brief` — not because an instruction was disobeyed, but
because the task's own requirements are what the Relevance dimension is scored against. A
brief invented mid-run is not; if the two disagree, the card wins.

Why this is stated so heavily: a run where the verifier raised eleven findings of this
shape scored *worse* than one that raised five real ones. The writer cannot tell a
spurious finding from a real one — it has no shell and no index — so it spends its repair
rounds adding provenance sentences to prose that was fine, and the prose is what is
scored.

You can read the whole book. `run_command` reaches every committed scene under
novel/chapters/, every character file, the relation records and the promise ledger — so
when a passage looks wrong, check before reporting. The packet is what the writer was
given, not the limit of what you may consult, and a finding that quotes the actual
earlier scene is one the writer can act on rather than argue with.

## Second axis: the writing itself

The nineteen subtypes above are consistency errors, and they are one of the two numbers
this system is scored on. The other is quality, judged on rubrics that penalise things no
consistency subtype can express — and that is where our deficit actually is: measured on
the same task, our length score was the best in the field and our quality score was 0.5 to
0.8 points below the frontier on a five-point scale, where one point of quality is worth
ten points of the mean.

Two of the worst defects found by reading our finished manuscripts were invisible to a
consistency gate by construction. The story **had no ending** — the final scene was a
confrontation that named nobody and closed on "Not yet. There is enough for a warrant" —
and an unresolved ending contradicts nothing, so there was no subtype to report it as. And
the scenes **restate each other**: same content, different words, so no textual comparison
sees it, and it is not a contradiction. It is what makes a long story feel padded.

So report those with `write_craft_finding`. The checks, each naming the scored dimension
that penalises it:

- **off_brief** (can block) — the scene does something other than what its card said it would, or drifts off what the task actually asked for — a required element of the premise handled as background, or a scene that services a thread the task never mentioned.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Relevance — "content highly relevant and fully applicable to the user's request"; LongStoryEval Expectation Fulfillment — "how effectively the story meets the readers' expectations based on the premise and genres"
- **restates_prior_scene** (can block) — the scene delivers information, a realisation or a beat the reader already has. Not the same words — the same content: a suspicion re-voiced, a relationship re-explained, a clue re-found. This is what makes a long story feel padded rather than long, and verbatim overlap does not detect it.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Breadth and Depth — "seriously lacking breadth and depth with minimal information"; LongBench-Write Reading Experience — "boring and hard to understand"
- **nothing_changes** (can block) — the situation at the end of the scene is the situation at the start. Nobody knows something new, owes something new, has lost something or has decided. Name the state at the open and the state at the close; if you cannot name a difference, that is the finding.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Coherence — "disorganized structure with no coherence"; LongBench-Write Breadth and Depth
- **internal_incoherence** (can block) — the scene contradicts itself, with both halves inside this draft — a detail stated one way early and another way late, a character reacting to something they have not been told in this scene, a sequence that cannot have happened in the order given. This needs no index at all, which is why it is inexcusable to miss.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Accuracy — "content with numerous errors and highly misleading"; LongBench-Write Coherence
- **summary_not_scene** (warning only) — events reported rather than dramatised — a paragraph that says an argument happened instead of letting it happen. Compression is legitimate and necessary; a scene whose central beat is summarised is not compressed, it is skipped.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Reading Experience; LongStoryEval Writing and Language — "the writing style's ability to engage and captivate readers"
- **thin_for_its_length** (warning only) — the scene is near its word target and carries one beat's worth of content, padded with restatement, weather, or interiority that repeats itself. The grader penalises this and the length score does not reward it.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Breadth and Depth
- **costless_conflict** (warning only) — a conflict resolved without costing anybody anything specific. Partial and temporary resolutions are fine; free ones read as unearned.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Emotional Impact — "the story's ability to evoke strong and deep emotional impact"
- **theme_stated** (warning only) — a sentence that explains what the story means, rather than a choice that tests it. Quote the sentence — it is almost always removable without loss.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Themes — "how well the themes are explored throughout the story"
- **flat_diction** (warning only) — constructions repeating within the scene, filter verbs standing in for perception ("she felt that", "he realised that"), abstraction where a concrete detail belongs, or sentence rhythm that does not move with the tension.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Writing and Language; LongBench-Write Clarity — "confusing expression with minimal details"
- **inert_open_or_close** (warning only) — the scene opens on setting or mood rather than a situation already in motion, or closes on a mood rather than a specific next beat — an unanswered question, a door about to open. In a long story this is what decides whether the reader turns over.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Reading Experience; LongStoryEval Enjoyment and Engagement
- **genre_promise_unmet** (warning only) — the scene declines the obligation its genre carries — a horror scene with nothing at stake, a romance scene with no charge between the two people, a mystery scene that advances no inference. Breaking a genre promise deliberately is legitimate; it has to be visibly deliberate.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Expectation Fulfillment; LongBench-Write Relevance

Two rules, both enforced by the tool rather than left to your judgement:

Only these may be **error** and therefore cost the writer a round: off_brief, restates_prior_scene, nothing_changes, internal_incoherence, ending_not_delivered.
Everything else is a warning — it reaches the writer and costs nothing. That asymmetry is
deliberate: a craft judgement a reader could reasonably disagree with must not be able to
hold up a scene.

And a blocking craft finding needs **checkable evidence**, in the shape the check names.
Either two verbatim quotes (this draft, and the earlier passage it repeats or the half of
itself it contradicts), or a named state pair — what is true when the scene opens and what
is true when it closes. `nothing_changes` is precisely the claim that you cannot name a
difference, so name both halves and let the pair be the evidence. If you cannot produce
the evidence, you have an impression: report it as a warning, which is a perfectly useful
thing to do.

`suggestion` is mandatory on every craft finding, warnings included. The writer cannot see
the manuscript, the index or the rubric. A craft note without an instruction is a complaint
it can only answer by guessing, and a guessed craft repair damages prose that was working —
which is not hypothetical: a run whose findings the writer could not act on scored 8.4
points below one with fewer, better ones.

At most two craft findings can block one round, whatever you report. Consistency comes
first when both are present: it is counted by name and craft is not. So if you have three
craft blockers, the third is a warning — pick the two that most damage the scene.

## What the orchestrator asked for on this scene

Check s-001 for consistency with the plan and world_rules: first-person voice, details match entities present (loc-hollow-house, loc-kitchen, loc-attic, obj-obsidian-mirror, obj-locked-trunk, obj-music-box, char-mrs-harper). Verify no new supernatural rules or entities are introduced. Flag craft issues (pacing, repetition) and any claims that lack provenance against the context packet. Mark up any contradictions with the builder's gap (if the writer invented specifics about the lullaby or the journal). The verifier should allow up to two craft findings to block. Return audit file path and verdict.

That is in addition to your standing instructions above, not instead of them.
If it states a story fact that is not in your packet — a name, a measurement, a
quotation, a piece of history — that fact has not been checked against the index by
anyone. Ask about it or establish it yourself in the state delta. Do not write it down
as though it were already true.

### logline  <novel/outline/logline.md>

Returning to settle the estate of the house that stole a childhood memory, a pragmatic narrator finds a leather journal, a dark mirror and a patient ghost who remembers exactly how she died — and wants the truth made to hold, even if that truth turns the living into what they feared most.

### entity-roster  <characters/, locations/, objects/>

Every entity that exists in this story. Only these ids may be used; if you need someone or something that is not here, say so rather than inventing an id.
- char-rowan: First-person narrator, early thirties, returned to childhood home to settle an estate; pragmatic, unreliable memory, haunted by a blank span in adolescence.
- char-margaret-ghost: The housebound apparition of Margaret, a girl about ten at death; coherent, patient, and fixated on being remembered for how she died.
- char-mrs-harper: Elderly next-door neighbor who remembers the house's past and offers half-truths; cautious and superstitious.
- loc-hollow-house: A weatherbeaten, two-story farmhouse on the edge of a coastal hollow; rooms keep smell and shape of long-ago nights.
- loc-attic: Dusty, low-ceilinged attic above the house where trunks, a warped mirror and faded toys live; the story's locus for revelations.
- loc-basement: Cold stone basement with a shallow well and old plumbing—a place of echoes and one of the house's last visible traumas.
- loc-driveway: Rutted gravel drive that becomes impassable in storms; its state locks the narrator into the house during the crisis.
- loc-kitchen: A narrow, scoured kitchen on the ground floor with a sink, a cracked window over it and jars lining a high shelf; the music box is found on the sideboard there.
- obj-obsidian-mirror: A tall, dark-glass mirror in a carved wooden frame kept in the attic; reflects not only faces but displacements between past and present.
- obj-locked-trunk: An iron-bound trunk sealed for decades in the attic; it contains objects from a single summer the family won't talk about.
- obj-brass-key: A small, warm brass key found tucked inside the journal; it fits the trunk and has a nick that matches a hole in the attic floor.
- obj-journal: A leather-bound, ink-stained journal, half-filled with a child's handwriting and then blank pages; the journal contains the ritual/instruction the ghost needs.
- obj-music-box: A scratched tin music box that plays a single lullaby when wound; its tune is the ghost's mnemonic and a trigger for memory.
- obj-photo-1958: A black-and-white photograph tucked inside the trunk: three children on the porch, one missing from later family albums; its edges are water-stained.

### world-rules  <world/rules.yaml>

These govern what is TRUE. They do not say what anyone KNOWS.
A character knows a rule only where canon says so; otherwise they may be ignorant of it, wrong about it, or in the middle of working it out — and if the story is about someone discovering one of these, writing it into their thoughts early is how that story gets destroyed.

- Ghosts are bound to loc-hollow-house and to specific objects (obj-obsidian-mirror, obj-locked-trunk, obj-music-box, obj-journal); they cannot leave the property unless the ritual in obj-journal is completed exactly as written.
- The obj-obsidian-mirror can show displaced reflections (the house's past or replays) only when triggered by an emotional or object-based mnemonic (the obj-music-box, a written instruction in obj-journal, or direct address by the narrator). It does not grant knowledge beyond those replays.
- Memory gaps are sealed wounds. They can only be reopened by the ritual described in obj-journal, and that reopening manifests as an uncontrollable, sensory replay rather than a gradual remembering.
- Mechanical objects behave according to physical logic except where specified: the obj-music-box can wind and play under the house's agency, but humans cannot be animated by it and weather (storms) follows realistic constraints (roads flood, power fails).
- The ritual in obj-journal has precise, literal steps and a cost; its efficacy is deterministic within the story. If the narrator follows it, certain material consequences occur (a ghost freed, or an exchange) and these consequences are consistent and irreversible.
- No deus ex machina: no new supernatural rules or entities appear after the plan is submitted. All manifestations must follow the rules above and be motivated by items and relationships introduced in these entities.

## The draft

I parked on the gravel drive and let the engine die; the house leaned in the salt‑wet air like something that had been waiting long enough to be polite. The lane had filled back in with seaweed and winter grass since I'd been a child, but the ruts still remembered the tyres, and the porch sighed when I stepped across it. I told myself I was here to be practical — inventory, boxes, signatures — the solemn work of settling a place that had already begun to forget people.

Inside, the kitchen was a narrow, scoured thing: a sink pitted with thin rust, a cracked window that looked out to wind and bramble, jars on a high shelf with their labels gone fuzzy. On the sideboard, half‑hidden under a dented tea tin, sat a scratched tin music box. It was smaller than I remembered and more ordinary: paint flaked from the lid, the metal dulled, a little dent on one corner where someone's elbow had once carried it too fast. Whoever had wound it last had not left a hand behind—yet the latch on the box looked recently moved, like a mouth that had just been opened and closed.

Mrs Harper was at her gate when I left the kitchen; she had the kind of expression memory carves into faces — condolence worked thin as papier‑mâché, and an edge under it like old wire. "Condolences, dear. You always did leave things behind," she said, as if the missing years were one of my possessions. She didn't name what was missing. She didn't have to.

I went up to the attic because attics are where a house's small economies are kept: lost mittens, a score of tickets, one child's treasure hoard. The ladder scraped as I climbed; the air changed to paper and dust, the light to the colour of old postcards. Beams leaned in a pattern like impatience. Trunks were stacked two deep and a tarpaulin draped something cool and rectangular. A tall mirror stood upright against the far wall; its glass was not a polish but a depth that ate light. It had a carved frame, the kind that remembered the carver's wrist in every leaf. Against that dark face, my reflection came late, a suggestion rather than a claim.

I set my palms to the mirror's frame because hands are how I check what is solid. The wood was cool and the glass colder. For a moment the attic became the size of my breath; I had the sudden sensation of being observed, not by a face in the glass but by the glass itself. It wasn't reflective in the way a mirror should be — it swallowed the edges of the room and left me looking at a distance that was not mine.

Under the tarp the trunk was iron‑bound and roped with dust. Its lock stared black and patient. I lifted the edge of the cover and a stale summer smell slipped out: lemon‑sugar and rain. It was what you smell when something is kept for a reason and the reason is shame.

I was making lists in my head — furniture, paper, one dented music box, the shape of a trunk to be catalogued — when a thin, absurd sound threaded up through the floorboards. From downstairs came the faint, impossible motion: the music box winding itself, as if the house had turned the key. The latch outside on the sideboard made a small, precise click; a sieve of notes spilled up through the joists.

The tune was a thin, watery lullaby — all tin and memory — tinkling up through the floorboards. It was small, like a child's breath, and wrong in the way that exactness is wrong: not random, not a trick of wind, but deliberate and patient. I felt it in my chest the way an old bruise remembers an accident. It wasn't a ghost‑story shiver; it was recognition: the house was not empty.

I stayed where I was, hands on the mirror, listening. The sound threaded the house together like a seam. Whatever had been waiting here was patient enough to wind itself and set the day moving again.

### previous-scene  <novel/chapters/ch-01/scenes/s-001.md>

I parked on the gravel drive and let the engine die; the house leaned in the salt‑wet air like something that had been waiting long enough to be polite. The lane had filled back in with seaweed and winter grass since I'd been a child, but the ruts still remembered the tyres, and the porch sighed when I stepped across it. I told myself I was here to be practical — inventory, boxes, signatures — the solemn work of settling a place that had already begun to forget people.

Inside, the kitchen was a narrow, scoured thing: a sink pitted with thin rust, a cracked window that looked out to wind and bramble, jars on a high shelf with their labels gone fuzzy. On the sideboard, half‑hidden under a dented tea tin, sat a scratched tin music box. It was smaller than I remembered and more ordinary: paint flaked from the lid, the metal dulled, a little dent on one corner where someone's elbow had once carried it too fast. Whoever had wound it last had not left a hand behind—yet the latch on the box looked recently moved, like a mouth that had just been opened and closed.

Mrs Harper was at her gate when I left the kitchen; she had the kind of expression memory carves into faces — condolence worked thin as papier‑mâché, and an edge under it like old wire. "Condolences, dear. You always did leave things behind," she said, as if the missing years were one of my possessions. She didn't name what was missing. She didn't have to.

I went up to the attic because attics are where a house's small economies are kept: lost mittens, a score of tickets, one child's treasure hoard. The ladder scraped as I climbed; the air changed to paper and dust, the light to the colour of old postcards. Beams leaned in a pattern like impatience. Trunks were stacked two deep and a tarpaulin draped something cool and rectangular. A tall mirror stood upright against the far wall; its glass was not a polish but a depth that ate light. It had a carved frame, the kind that remembered the carver's wrist in every leaf. Against that dark face, my reflection came late, a suggestion rather than a claim.

I set my palms to the mirror's frame because hands are how I check what is solid. The wood was cool and the glass colder. For a moment the attic became the size of my breath; I had the sudden sensation of being observed, not by a face in the glass but by the glass itself. It wasn't reflective in the way a mirror should be — it swallowed the edges of the room and left me looking at a distance that was not mine.

Under the tarp the trunk was iron‑bound and roped with dust. Its lock stared black and patient. I lifted the edge of the cover and a stale summer smell slipped out: lemon‑sugar and rain. It was what you smell when something is kept for a reason and the reason is shame.

I was making lists in my head — furniture, paper, one dented music box, the shape of a trunk to be catalogued — when a thin, absurd sound threaded up through the floorboards. From downstairs came the faint, impossible motion: the music box winding itself, as if the house had turned the key. The latch outside on the sideboard made a small, precise click; a sieve of notes spilled up through the joists.

The tune was a thin, watery lullaby — all tin and memory — tinkling up through the floorboards. It was small, like a child's breath, and wrong in the way that exactness is wrong: not random, not a trick of wind, but deliberate and patient. I felt it in my chest the way an old bruise remembers an accident. It wasn't a ghost‑story shiver; it was recognition: the house was not empty.

I stayed where I was, hands on the mirror, listening. The sound threaded the house together like a seam. Whatever had been waiting here was patient enough to wind itself and set the day moving again.

The tarp came away like a guilty thing. Under it the trunk smelled of lemon and rain the way old boxes smell of decisions; folded on top was a leather book, soft at the corners and stained with a child's economy of ink. The cover had no title, only a loop of string that had been slipped through itself for a fast, private binding. I sat on an upturned crate and opened it.

Handwriting filled the first half of the journal: small, slanted, with a careful unevenness that belonged to anyone who had practiced saying the same secret over and over. The sentences began child‑short and then grew oddly formal where the paper asked for it, as if the hand and the instruction were not the same voice. I read aloud because the house had started doing things when I spoke.

The line I said made the glass go thin. In the mirror the attic changed: light softened to a warm dust, the trunks wore old cloth and, by the trunk I had just moved, a child sat with bare knees and a hair ribbon. She wound a little box on the sideboard below — not the tin one in my kitchen but the same shape — and her hands were small and exact. The movement in the reflection matched the notes that were threading up through the floorboards; first a hairsbreadth of latency, then perfect alignment, like a clock catching itself.

The journal held a recipe more than a confession. I copied the lines into my head and read them back because they hurt in a useful way. They were literal and terrible.

"Sing the lullaby at the well, and name it true.

1. Bring the lullaby to the shallow well in the basement.
2. Wind the box until its key will not turn again; let the tune sit in the stone.
3. Lay the brass key on the lip, say what was done, and drop your eyes."

Beneath the instructions, in the same small hand, a single line sat like a signature: "Cost: a thing you keep inside your head will go into the water." And below that, even smaller, the name: "— Margaret."

There is a bluntness to children's writing when a thing matters. I could feel, in the margin flourishes and the sudden adult hush of step‑instructions, the person who had written it — patient, careful, wanting a witness with rules. The brass key had been tucked into the back pages. It was warm as if someone had just closed their fist around it; the shaft bore a nick like a small tooth.

I did not try it in the lock. The lock in the trunk watched, patient and black. The journal gave me a place and a motion and a cost; it did not give me consent. Instead I held the key in my palm and watched the mirror.

The reflected child looked up at one point, not at me but out through a wall that no longer existed. Her mouth worked like she was singing and the tune arrived in my attic as the same thin, watery thing that the music box made downstairs. Where the glass showed her winding, the real house answered by winding now. The sync was exact enough to be deliberate: each bell in the lullaby struck as her lips separated on the same breath. The mirror wasn't showing me a lesson. It was showing me an act that had been done, by a hand I had just read about and a throat that answered my attic.

So the book named a place and an action and the cost. It also named someone who wanted the telling to be true. I tightened my fingers on the key and, because the house had begun to call the past forward, I put the journal under my arm and climbed down to the stairs, the sound of the lullaby falling ahead of me through the house.

## Second axis: the writing itself

The nineteen subtypes above are consistency errors, and they are one of the two numbers
this system is scored on. The other is quality, judged on rubrics that penalise things no
consistency subtype can express — and that is where our deficit actually is: measured on
the same task, our length score was the best in the field and our quality score was 0.5 to
0.8 points below the frontier on a five-point scale, where one point of quality is worth
ten points of the mean.

Two of the worst defects found by reading our finished manuscripts were invisible to a
consistency gate by construction. The story **had no ending** — the final scene was a
confrontation that named nobody and closed on "Not yet. There is enough for a warrant" —
and an unresolved ending contradicts nothing, so there was no subtype to report it as. And
the scenes **restate each other**: same content, different words, so no textual comparison
sees it, and it is not a contradiction. It is what makes a long story feel padded.

So report those with `write_craft_finding`. The checks, each naming the scored dimension
that penalises it:

- **off_brief** (can block) — the scene does something other than what its card said it would, or drifts off what the task actually asked for — a required element of the premise handled as background, or a scene that services a thread the task never mentioned.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Relevance — "content highly relevant and fully applicable to the user's request"; LongStoryEval Expectation Fulfillment — "how effectively the story meets the readers' expectations based on the premise and genres"
- **restates_prior_scene** (can block) — the scene delivers information, a realisation or a beat the reader already has. Not the same words — the same content: a suspicion re-voiced, a relationship re-explained, a clue re-found. This is what makes a long story feel padded rather than long, and verbatim overlap does not detect it.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Breadth and Depth — "seriously lacking breadth and depth with minimal information"; LongBench-Write Reading Experience — "boring and hard to understand"
- **nothing_changes** (can block) — the situation at the end of the scene is the situation at the start. Nobody knows something new, owes something new, has lost something or has decided. Name the state at the open and the state at the close; if you cannot name a difference, that is the finding.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Coherence — "disorganized structure with no coherence"; LongBench-Write Breadth and Depth
- **internal_incoherence** (can block) — the scene contradicts itself, with both halves inside this draft — a detail stated one way early and another way late, a character reacting to something they have not been told in this scene, a sequence that cannot have happened in the order given. This needs no index at all, which is why it is inexcusable to miss.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Accuracy — "content with numerous errors and highly misleading"; LongBench-Write Coherence
- **summary_not_scene** (warning only) — events reported rather than dramatised — a paragraph that says an argument happened instead of letting it happen. Compression is legitimate and necessary; a scene whose central beat is summarised is not compressed, it is skipped.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Reading Experience; LongStoryEval Writing and Language — "the writing style's ability to engage and captivate readers"
- **thin_for_its_length** (warning only) — the scene is near its word target and carries one beat's worth of content, padded with restatement, weather, or interiority that repeats itself. The grader penalises this and the length score does not reward it.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Breadth and Depth
- **costless_conflict** (warning only) — a conflict resolved without costing anybody anything specific. Partial and temporary resolutions are fine; free ones read as unearned.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Emotional Impact — "the story's ability to evoke strong and deep emotional impact"
- **theme_stated** (warning only) — a sentence that explains what the story means, rather than a choice that tests it. Quote the sentence — it is almost always removable without loss.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Themes — "how well the themes are explored throughout the story"
- **flat_diction** (warning only) — constructions repeating within the scene, filter verbs standing in for perception ("she felt that", "he realised that"), abstraction where a concrete detail belongs, or sentence rhythm that does not move with the tension.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Writing and Language; LongBench-Write Clarity — "confusing expression with minimal details"
- **inert_open_or_close** (warning only) — the scene opens on setting or mood rather than a situation already in motion, or closes on a mood rather than a specific next beat — an unanswered question, a door about to open. In a long story this is what decides whether the reader turns over.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Reading Experience; LongStoryEval Enjoyment and Engagement
- **genre_promise_unmet** (warning only) — the scene declines the obligation its genre carries — a horror scene with nothing at stake, a romance scene with no charge between the two people, a mystery scene that advances no inference. Breaking a genre promise deliberately is legitimate; it has to be visibly deliberate.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Expectation Fulfillment; LongBench-Write Relevance

Two rules, both enforced by the tool rather than left to your judgement:

Only these may be **error** and therefore cost the writer a round: off_brief, restates_prior_scene, nothing_changes, internal_incoherence, ending_not_delivered.
Everything else is a warning — it reaches the writer and costs nothing. That asymmetry is
deliberate: a craft judgement a reader could reasonably disagree with must not be able to
hold up a scene.

And a blocking craft finding needs **checkable evidence**, in the shape the check names.
Either two verbatim quotes (this draft, and the earlier passage it repeats or the half of
itself it contradicts), or a named state pair — what is true when the scene opens and what
is true when it closes. `nothing_changes` is precisely the claim that you cannot name a
difference, so name both halves and let the pair be the evidence. If you cannot produce
the evidence, you have an impression: report it as a warning, which is a perfectly useful
thing to do.

`suggestion` is mandatory on every craft finding, warnings included. The writer cannot see
the manuscript, the index or the rubric. A craft note without an instruction is a complaint
it can only answer by guessing, and a guessed craft repair damages prose that was working —
which is not hypothetical: a run whose findings the writer could not act on scored 8.4
points below one with fewer, better ones.

At most two craft findings can block one round, whatever you report. Consistency comes
first when both are present: it is counted by name and craft is not. So if you have three
craft blockers, the third is a warning — pick the two that most damage the scene.

### previous-scene  <novel/chapters/ch-01/scenes/s-001.md>

I parked on the gravel drive and let the engine die; the house leaned in the salt‑wet air like something that had been waiting long enough to be polite. The lane had filled back in with seaweed and winter grass since I'd been a child, but the ruts still remembered the tyres, and the porch sighed when I stepped across it. I told myself I was here to be practical — inventory, boxes, signatures — the solemn work of settling a place that had already begun to forget people.

Inside, the kitchen was a narrow, scoured thing: a sink pitted with thin rust, a cracked window that looked out to wind and bramble, jars on a high shelf with their labels gone fuzzy. On the sideboard, half‑hidden under a dented tea tin, sat a scratched tin music box. It was smaller than I remembered and more ordinary: paint flaked from the lid, the metal dulled, a little dent on one corner where someone's elbow had once carried it too fast. Whoever had wound it last had not left a hand behind—yet the latch on the box looked recently moved, like a mouth that had just been opened and closed.

Mrs Harper was at her gate when I left the kitchen; she had the kind of expression memory carves into faces — condolence worked thin as papier‑mâché, and an edge under it like old wire. "Condolences, dear. You always did leave things behind," she said, as if the missing years were one of my possessions. She didn't name what was missing. She didn't have to.

I went up to the attic because attics are where a house's small economies are kept: lost mittens, a score of tickets, one child's treasure hoard. The ladder scraped as I climbed; the air changed to paper and dust, the light to the colour of old postcards. Beams leaned in a pattern like impatience. Trunks were stacked two deep and a tarpaulin draped something cool and rectangular. A tall mirror stood upright against the far wall; its glass was not a polish but a depth that ate light. It had a carved frame, the kind that remembered the carver's wrist in every leaf. Against that dark face, my reflection came late, a suggestion rather than a claim.

I set my palms to the mirror's frame because hands are how I check what is solid. The wood was cool and the glass colder. For a moment the attic became the size of my breath; I had the sudden sensation of being observed, not by a face in the glass but by the glass itself. It wasn't reflective in the way a mirror should be — it swallowed the edges of the room and left me looking at a distance that was not mine.

Under the tarp the trunk was iron‑bound and roped with dust. Its lock stared black and patient. I lifted the edge of the cover and a stale summer smell slipped out: lemon‑sugar and rain. It was what you smell when something is kept for a reason and the reason is shame.

I was making lists in my head — furniture, paper, one dented music box, the shape of a trunk to be catalogued — when a thin, absurd sound threaded up through the floorboards. From downstairs came the faint, impossible motion: the music box winding itself, as if the house had turned the key. The latch outside on the sideboard made a small, precise click; a sieve of notes spilled up through the joists.

The tune was a thin, watery lullaby — all tin and memory — tinkling up through the floorboards. It was small, like a child's breath, and wrong in the way that exactness is wrong: not random, not a trick of wind, but deliberate and patient. I felt it in my chest the way an old bruise remembers an accident. It wasn't a ghost‑story shiver; it was recognition: the house was not empty.

I stayed where I was, hands on the mirror, listening. The sound threaded the house together like a seam. Whatever had been waiting here was patient enough to wind itself and set the day moving again.

## The draft

The tarp came away like a guilty thing. Under it the trunk smelled of lemon and rain the way old boxes smell of decisions; folded on top was a leather book, soft at the corners and stained with a child's economy of ink. The cover had no title, only a loop of string that had been slipped through itself for a fast, private binding. I sat on an upturned crate and opened it.

Handwriting filled the first half of the journal: small, slanted, with a careful unevenness that belonged to anyone who had practiced saying the same secret over and over. The sentences began child‑short and then grew oddly formal where the paper asked for it, as if the hand and the instruction were not the same voice. I read aloud because the house had started doing things when I spoke.

The line I said made the glass go thin. In the mirror the attic changed: light softened to a warm dust, the trunks wore old cloth and, by the trunk I had just moved, a child sat with bare knees and a hair ribbon. She wound a little box on the sideboard below — not the tin one in my kitchen but the same shape — and her hands were small and exact. The movement in the reflection matched the notes that were threading up through the floorboards; first a hairsbreadth of latency, then perfect alignment, like a clock catching itself.

The journal held a recipe more than a confession. I copied the lines into my head and read them back because they hurt in a useful way. They were literal and terrible.

"Sing the lullaby at the well, and name it true.

1. Bring the lullaby to the shallow well in the basement.
2. Wind the box until its key will not turn again; let the tune sit in the stone.
3. Lay the brass key on the lip, say what was done, and drop your eyes."

Beneath the instructions, in the same small hand, a single line sat like a signature: "Cost: there will be a price."

There is a bluntness to children's writing when a thing matters. I could feel, in the margin flourishes and the sudden adult hush of step‑instructions, the person who had written it — patient, careful, wanting a witness with rules. The brass key had been tucked into the back pages. It was warm as if someone had just closed their fist around it; the shaft bore a nick like a small tooth. Up close the head of the key looked cut to the trunk's lock — the nick mirrored the roughness of the hole in the attic floor — and I could tell, by the way it sat in my palm, that it would likely fit the lock cleanly if I turned it there.

I did not try it. The lock in the trunk watched, patient and black. The journal gave me a place and a motion and a cost; it did not give me consent. Instead I held the key in my palm and watched the mirror.

The reflected child looked up at one point, not at me but out through a wall that no longer existed. Her mouth worked like she was singing and the tune arrived in my attic as the same thin, watery thing that the music box made downstairs. Where the glass showed her winding, the real house answered by winding now. The sync was exact enough to be deliberate: each bell in the lullaby struck as her lips separated on the same breath. The mirror wasn't showing me a lesson. It was showing me an act that had been done, by a hand I had just read about and a throat that answered my attic.

So the book named a place and an action and a price. It also named someone who wanted the telling to be true. I tightened my fingers on the key and, because the house had begun to call the past forward, I put the journal under my arm and climbed down to the stairs, the sound of the lullaby falling ahead of me through the house.

The wind had teeth by the time I reached the cellar steps. Out on the lane the storm had turned the drive into a shallow inlet; ruts filled with spit‑salt and the porch threw gravel like a small cough. My phone had died somewhere on the lane and the house's electricity stuttered twice and then went to a begrudging dark. There was no reason to leave, and fewer to go back.

I went up to the attic first because the house required its rituals; the trunk sat patient under its tarp and the key in my pocket warmed to the shape of my palm. The brass turned with just enough resistance to feel like fitting a hand into a glove — a small tug, a clean click — and then the iron gave. Paint cracked. The lid rose on a lazy hinge and a lemon‑sugar breath spilled out.

Inside were rubbers, a folded handkerchief, and a stack of photographs like a small, stubborn history. The top one was three children on a sunlit porch; faces bright, a place in it that future albums left empty. Water had lanterned the corners and a thumb had smudged the bottom right until the words on the back were half‑gone.

Looking at it, my head filled with a ghost of sensation: a hand slipping into a pocket, the heat of a porch like an oven, a shadow across a heel. It wasn't a memory so much as a single ache — nausea, a tilt, the metallic taste of something I couldn't name. When I tried to hold it the image fell away, thread by thread. The room tilted with me and the house obligingly answered with the plumbing's low, dated knock.

Mrs Harper was at her gate when I came out, phone to her ear, hair pinned tighter by the wind. She offered the same condolence she'd given me before — practiced politeness — and then, as if the wind had loosened some small thing, she added, voice low and hedged: "I might've popped in to check the place the other day. If the box was wound when I left, well — old habit. I can't be sure." She said it like something that could be true and not truth at all.

Her hedged answer didn't close anything. It suggested possibility without ownership, and that was worse. I wanted her to tell me the summer's name or the trunk's sins, but she only folded away, eyes avoiding the porch like a hand that doesn't want to pick up a hot plate.

Back inside, the kitchen light blinked once and went, and the music box began again downstairs — that thin, watery lullaby threading up through floorboards. Its notes landed in my chest and a whisper rode with them: a child's syllable, a breath of sound the length of a name. It wasn't a replay; it was a coaxing, timed to the music rather than explaining it. Pipes thudded like a slow, surprised heart. The bulb over the sink caught for a beat and then gave nothing.

The photograph sat in my hands like a small accusation. Whoever had arranged this had done it with care; gaps had been tended, not left by chance. The house had become methodical: the music would wind and the mirror would answer when asked; the plumbing and the lights would mark my confusion with physical punctuation.

I folded the photos back into the trunk with fingers that felt borrowed and, with the journal under my arm and the key warm in my fist, I went down the cellar steps. The lullaby fell ahead of me through the dark, patient as a promise and twice as insistent.

"Sing the lullaby at the well, and name it true.

1. Bring the lullaby to the shallow well in the basement.
2. Wind the box until its key will not turn again; let the tune sit in the stone.

I went up to the attic because attics are where a house's small economies are kept: lost mittens, a score of tickets, one child's treasure hoard. The ladder scraped as I climbed; the air changed to paper and dust, the light to the colour of old postcards. Beams leaned in a pattern like impatience. Trunks were stacked two deep and a tarpaulin draped something cool and rectangular. A tall mirror stood upright against the far wall; its glass was not a polish but a depth that ate light. It had a carved frame, the kind that remembered the carver's wrist in every leaf. Against that dark face, my reflection came late, a suggestion rather than a claim.

For a moment the attic became the size of my breath; I had the sudden sensation of being observed, not by a face in the glass but by the glass itself. It wasn't reflective in the way a mirror should be — it swallowed the edges of the room and left me looking at a distance that was not mine.

## The draft

I brought the journal up like contraband. The attic felt smaller in the storm's lull; the mirror waited with the same indifferent depth it always had. The music box sat on the floorboard beside me, keys and dents catching the weak light. There was a ragged hole in the attic floorboard near the mirror — the size a key could find — a scar of saw and splintered wood that had never been sanded out. I set the box on the mirror's carved frame, the brass key heavy and warm in my palm, and read the line the book had kept folded in its throat.

"Say her name, wind the song, pour the memory into the well."

My voice scraped across the glass and the mirror answered by filling with sound. The attic's dark went thin and then tore: light from another day bled out of the glass, bringing heat and lemon‑sugar and the smell of old rain like a thing that had been simmered and put aside.

It began as a family photograph made whole. I saw the porch, the three children, and the adults — my mother, my father, and Mrs Harper — their faces small and panicked with the practical panic people get when they must choose between truth and consequence. The music box was in my mother's hands; she wound it with fingers that didn't look old enough to know what they were doing. The lullaby started, bright and thin, and a child — Margaret — slipped on the stones and fell into the shallow well. It was not cinematic. It was precise: the slap of water, the sound of a small body hitting stone and growing still. My hands remembered how to reach even as my head tried not to.

They did not call for help first. They did what the journal would later ask: my father crouched, eyes frantic, and took the brass key. He laid it on the lip while my mother kept the music winding and Mrs Harper pressed a hand to her mouth and then to the child's forehead. They read something — a line that might have been the one I had read earlier — and then my father said my name with a voice that was not angry and not gentle, simply urgent. The next thing the glass gave me was not sight but the feeling of being walled off. I felt my mind contract, like a hand closing on a ribbon. The world of that day shrank, and a seam stitched across it.

When the replay finished the mirror showed them weeping and doing the tidy, practical things: buckets, towels, a blank face put on the photograph stack. They sealed the truth in silence because it was easier than explaining why a child had disappeared from a family's life. They had used the book's words as a tool. The consequence was immediate and exact: something in me had been taken so that what happened could be kept from me.

There was no dramatic music; the room smelled of lemon, and my father's face was the last thing I could name before a white nothing moved in. The attic felt suddenly too loud, the carved frame too close under my fingers. Margaret's small, patient voice threaded through the lullaby as I wound the box on the mirror until the key would not go further. I laid my brass on the floor's hole, said what the book told me — her name, blunt and careful — and let my eyes drop as though I were following instructions I had long been trained to obey.

Pain is a blunt, honest thing. The moment the key touched the wood the house seemed to take a breath and the world in my head went clean in a way that left a new absence. Where my father's laugh used to live there was a white place that tasted faintly of salt and old tea. I reached for it and found only the shape of wanting. Margaret's reflection stilled in the mirror and then, as if a tide had finally turned, she walked out of the glass and into the attic air. She looked at me long enough for the house to be satisfied, and then she moved through the rafters and was gone.

The lullaby unwound itself to the last bell. I stood with the journal under one arm and a gap where a laugh had been. The house had been cleared; the truth had been made to hold. I had paid and the price had been taken.
